x.A: Sending application data to Firehose is a delivery pipeline to a destination. It neither formats an HTML report nor schedules a daily email.
x.B: Amazon SES sends email to multiple recipients at once, and it can send an HTML message, so it handles the email part of the report.
x.C: Glue is an ETL service and is not a good fit for calling a REST API on a schedule and building a report. A Lambda function is simpler.
x.D: An EventBridge scheduled rule invoking Lambda runs every morning, calls the REST API, and builds the HTML report with no servers.
x.E: S3 event notifications fire when objects change, not on a daily schedule, and an SNS email contains the notification, not a formatted HTML report.

x.A: S3 is object storage, not a standard file system structure, so the application would have to be changed to use it.
x.B: EBS volumes are tied to one AZ, have a size limit, and do not scale automatically. They also attach to a single instance.
x.C: EFS is a POSIX file system that grows automatically to petabytes and is highly available across AZs. EC2 in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group keeps the compute available with little management.
x.D: EBS has a size limit and is AZ-bound, so it cannot hold hundreds of terabytes or scale automatically.

x.A: Glacier with an access control policy can be changed by an administrator or root user, so it does not guarantee that nobody can delete the records.
x.B: An IAM policy can be edited by administrators, and Intelligent-Tiering does not archive for the last 9 years as cheaply. Nothing here prevents root deletion.
x.C: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode prevents any user, including root, from deleting or overwriting objects for the retention period. A lifecycle rule to Glacier Deep Archive after a year is cheap, and it is stored across multiple AZs.
x.D: Governance mode lets users with special permissions bypass the lock, and One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so it is not maximum resiliency.

x.A: Moving to S3 with IAM authentication changes how users access files. They use Windows file shares today, which S3 doesn't provide.
x.B: An S3 File Gateway mounted on EC2 doesn't give the same native Windows file share experience with a highly available Multi-AZ design.
x.C: FSx for Windows File Server gives native SMB file shares with Active Directory integration. A Multi-AZ setup is highly available and durable, and users keep accessing files the same way.
x.D: EFS uses NFS and does not support SMB for Windows clients, so it would change the access method.

x.A: Route tables control where traffic goes, not who may connect. Within a VPC the local route always exists, so removing a route to the public subnets does not restrict access to the database.
x.B: Security groups can only allow traffic, not deny it, so a group that denies inbound traffic is not possible.
x.C: Security groups can reference other security groups. Allowing inbound traffic to the DB security group only from the private-subnet instances' security group restricts access to just those instances.
x.D: VPC peering connects separate VPCs and does not control access between subnets in one VPC.

x.A: Stage variables pass configuration values to an API and do not override the default invoke URL or provide a custom domain.
x.B: A Regional endpoint needs the certificate in ACM in the same Region as the API, not in us-east-1, and an alias to a stage endpoint does not create a custom domain on API Gateway.
x.C: For a Regional API Gateway endpoint, you create a custom domain name, import the certificate into ACM in the same Region (ca-central-1), attach it, and point Route 53 at the endpoint.
x.D: The us-east-1 certificate requirement applies to edge-optimized endpoints that use CloudFront, not to a Regional endpoint in ca-central-1.

x.A: Comprehend analyzes text and does not detect inappropriate images.
x.B: Rekognition has a built-in content moderation API for detecting inappropriate images, and human review of low-confidence results can be added. It needs almost no development.
x.C: SageMaker would require building and training a model, which is much more development effort.
x.D: Running a custom model on Fargate also needs a model to be built, deployed, and maintained, so it is a lot more work.

x.A: Installing Docker on EC2 instances means you manage the hosts yourself, including patching and scaling.
x.B: ECS on EC2 worker nodes still requires you to provision, patch, and scale the instances.
x.C: ECS on Fargate runs containers serverlessly, so there are no servers to provision or manage while still giving scalability and availability.
x.D: Using an ECS-optimized AMI still means managing EC2 instances, so the company remains responsible for the infrastructure.

x.A: Data Pipeline with an EMR cluster is a batch approach that needs cluster management and is not designed for 30 TB per day of streaming data.
x.B: An EC2 Auto Scaling group that processes the data is custom work to build and operate, and it does not provide the managed streaming ingestion needed.
x.C: CloudFront is for delivering content and caching, not for collecting clickstream data, and per-object Lambda processing does not scale well to this volume.
x.D: Kinesis Data Streams ingests very high-volume clickstream data in real time, Firehose delivers it to an S3 data lake, and Redshift analyzes it at scale.

x.A: Network ACLs allow or deny traffic and cannot redirect requests, so HTTP users would simply be blocked.
x.B: There is no simple rule that rewrites the URL scheme. The ALB redirect action does this.
x.C: An ALB listener rule on the HTTP (port 80) listener can redirect requests to HTTPS (port 443) natively.
x.D: An NLB works at layer 4 and does not do HTTP redirects. SNI is for choosing certificates, not redirecting.

x.A: Instance metadata is not meant for storing database credentials, and rotating them requires custom Lambda code.
x.B: A configuration file in S3 with a custom Lambda rotation requires building and maintaining the rotation logic and the file updates.
x.C: Secrets Manager stores credentials so they are not hardcoded, rotates RDS credentials automatically with built-in support, and the EC2 role is given access to the secret.
x.D: Parameter Store has no automatic rotation, so the rotation would have to be built separately.

x.A: ACM issues certificates from Amazon's own CA, not from an external CA, so this does not meet the requirement.
x.B: You cannot import key material into a certificate that ACM issued, and ACM-issued certificates do not come from an external CA.
x.C: ACM Private CA issues private certificates, which browsers do not trust for a public website, and it is not an external CA.
x.D: A certificate from an external CA has to be imported into ACM. Imported certificates are not renewed automatically, so EventBridge can send an expiration notice and the certificate is rotated manually.

x.A: S3 stores the originals and converted files cheaply at any scale, and an S3 PUT event invoking Lambda is a serverless converter that is billed only when used. It scales with growing demand.
x.B: DynamoDB has item size limits and is not designed or priced for storing large files.
x.C: Elastic Beanstalk with EC2, EBS, and Auto Scaling means paying for servers all the time and managing them, and EBS storage scales less well.
x.D: This has the same always-on EC2 cost and operations, and it uses EFS but then saves files to EBS, which is inconsistent and more expensive.

x.A: Moving everything to FSx in AWS gives the cloud workloads access but adds latency for on-premises users, who would have to reach the file system across the VPN.
x.B: An S3 File Gateway changes how cloud workloads access the data and is not a natural fit for Windows file shares.
x.C: Splitting workloads between S3 directly and the S3 File Gateway means changing file access patterns, which the question says to avoid.
x.D: FSx for Windows File Server serves the cloud workloads, and an on-premises FSx File Gateway caches frequently used data locally for low latency. The SMB access pattern stays the same.

x.A: Using Python libraries to extract text and identify PHI means writing and maintaining the code and models, so it has high operational effort.
x.B: Textract extracts the text, but SageMaker would require building and training a model for PHI detection.
x.C: Textract extracts text from PDF and image files, and Comprehend Medical has a built-in PHI detection API. Both are managed services that need no model training.
x.D: Rekognition is for image analysis and is not designed to extract document text for this purpose, though it can read some text in images.

x.A: Glacier has retrieval delays, so files would not be immediately accessible, which is a stated requirement.
x.B: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, which is risky for critical data that is not easy to reproduce.
x.C: Files stay immediately accessible and multi-AZ. Moving them to Standard-IA after 30 days lowers storage cost for rarely accessed data, and a rule deletes them after 4 years.
x.D: Moving to Glacier after 4 years is pointless because the files can be deleted at that point, and it adds retrieval cost and delay.

x.A: Creating a new queue does not change how long a message stays hidden, so it does not stop duplicate processing.
x.B: AddPermission changes who can use the queue and has no effect on duplicate processing.
x.C: Setting a wait time on ReceiveMessage enables long polling, which reduces empty responses and does not stop a message from reappearing.
x.D: If processing takes longer than the visibility timeout, the message becomes visible again and another instance processes it, which creates duplicate rows. Increasing the visibility timeout keeps the message hidden until processing finishes.

x.A: Direct Connect gives consistent low latency, and a Site-to-Site VPN backup is a low-cost failover that accepts slower traffic when Direct Connect fails.
x.B: Two VPN tunnels run over the internet, so latency is not consistent.
x.C: A second Direct Connect connection gives a fast backup, but it costs more than a VPN, and the question allows slower traffic on failover.
x.D: There is no Direct Connect failover attribute in the CLI that automatically creates a backup connection.

x.A: Multiple Regions with cross-Region replication is much more complex and operationally heavy than the requirement needs.
x.B: Spreading the Auto Scaling group across AZs and making the Aurora database Multi-AZ gives automatic failover with minimal downtime and data loss. RDS Proxy keeps connections smooth during a failover.
x.C: A single AZ with hourly snapshots means downtime during recovery and up to an hour of data loss.
x.D: Multiple Regions with S3 events writing to a database is a complex custom design and does not provide high availability for the database.

x.A: An NLB does not support HTTP health checks by URL in the way needed here. It checks at the TCP level and cannot detect HTTP application errors.
x.B: A cron job that scans logs and restarts the application is a custom script, which the question rules out.
x.C: An ALB supports HTTP health checks on a URL, and Auto Scaling can replace unhealthy instances automatically, with no custom scripts or code.
x.D: The NLB only sees TCP health, so UnhealthyHostCount will not reflect HTTP errors, and this would not detect the problem.

x.A: Global tables replicate changes to other Regions, including corrupted data, so they protect against Region failure and not against data corruption.
x.B: DynamoDB point-in-time recovery lets you restore a table to any second in the previous 35 days, which meets a 15-minute RPO, and restoring a table fits a 1-hour RTO.
x.C: Daily exports give an RPO of a day rather than 15 minutes, and Glacier restores are slow.
x.D: DynamoDB is a managed service with no EBS volumes to snapshot.

x.A: API Gateway is not a route target for S3 traffic, and it would add its own charges.
x.B: A NAT gateway charges for data processing and hourly use, which adds cost instead of reducing it, and gateway endpoint policies do not attach to a NAT gateway.
x.C: Routing through an internet gateway sends the traffic over the public path, and a public subnet exposes the application.
x.D: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 keeps traffic to S3 in the same Region on the AWS network with no NAT or internet gateway data processing charges, and an endpoint policy can restrict access.

x.A: The bastion host must accept connections from the company's network, not only from the application instances, so this would lock out the administrators.
x.B: The company's internal IP range is not what the bastion sees. Traffic arrives from the internet through the company's external address.
x.C: The bastion host is reached over the internet from the company's connection, so its security group should allow inbound SSH from the company's external IP range.
x.D: The bastion connects to the application servers over the private network, so their security group should allow SSH from the bastion's private IP address.
x.E: The bastion uses its private IP address inside the VPC to reach the instances in the private subnet, so the public IP would not match.

x.A: The public web tier must accept HTTPS from users anywhere, so inbound 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 is required.
x.B: Security groups are stateful, so responses to allowed inbound traffic are allowed automatically. This rule is not required to serve users.
x.C: The database tier should accept SQL Server traffic (port 1433) only from the web tier's security group, which keeps it closed to everything else.
x.D: Outbound rules from the database to the web tier are unnecessary because security groups are stateful, and port 443 is not needed.
x.E: Opening port 443 on the database tier is unnecessary, so it widens access beyond what the database needs.

x.A: API Gateway with Lambda is a serverless, auto-scaling application layer, and SQS between services buffers load so transactions are not dropped when a tier is overloaded.
x.B: Larger EC2 instances sized for past peaks do not remove the bottleneck, wastes money at other times, and does not modernize the application.
x.C: SNS is a pub/sub service, not a queue, so there is no queue length to monitor and messages are not buffered.
x.D: SQS works for buffering, but scaling up only when communication failures are detected is reactive, and managing EC2 and scaling is more operational effort than serverless.
